lesson.title: The Empirical Rule: Predicting Data Without a Calculator
lesson.summary: The empirical rule states that for approximately normal data, fixed and highly predictable percentages of values fall within one, two, and three standard deviations of the mean, letting you estimate probabilities using only the mean and standard deviation.
lesson.body:
One of the most useful consequences of a distribution being approximately normal is that you no longer need to see every individual data point to know roughly how the data behaves. Because every normal curve shares the same underlying bell shape, differing only in its mean and standard deviation, the proportion of data falling within a given number of standard deviations of the mean is always the same, no matter which specific normal distribution you are looking at. This consistent pattern is called the empirical rule, named because it was first observed by studying real, empirical data long before it was fully justified by the mathematics of the normal curve.

The name is worth pausing on. Empirical means based on observation, and long before statisticians had the calculus needed to describe the normal curve precisely, they noticed that repeated measurements of natural quantities, errors in astronomical observations, human heights, and similar variables, kept showing the same rough pattern: values piled up near the center and thinned out symmetrically on both sides, with a strikingly consistent share of the data staying within a small number of standard deviations of the mean. That observed regularity earned its own name well before it was proven to follow directly from the normal density function.

The rule itself works with any approximately normal distribution once you know just the mean and the standard deviation. As a first piece of it, roughly 68 percent of the data in a normal distribution falls within one standard deviation of the mean, meaning between the mean minus one standard deviation and the mean plus one standard deviation. Suppose a laptop model's battery life is approximately normal with a mean of 300 minutes and a standard deviation of 20 minutes. One standard deviation below the mean is 300 minus 20, or 280 minutes, and one standard deviation above the mean is 300 plus 20, or 320 minutes. The empirical rule says about 68 percent of these laptops should have a battery life between 280 and 320 minutes, a specific, checkable prediction that follows from knowing nothing more than the mean and the standard deviation.

What makes this genuinely powerful is that the same 68 percent figure applies to any normal distribution whatsoever, whether it describes battery life in minutes, heart rate in beats per minute, or exam scores on a 100-point scale. The only work required is finding the mean and standard deviation for the situation at hand and then measuring distances in standard deviations rather than in the original units. That is the core habit the empirical rule teaches: think in standard deviations, not raw numbers, and the same predictable percentages apply everywhere the normal model reasonably fits.

The one standard deviation figure of 68 percent is only the first layer of the rule. Two and three standard deviations from the mean come with their own fixed, and even larger, percentages, which together with the 68 percent figure form the complete quantitative statement of the empirical rule, covered in full detail next.
